SHAREHOLDER AND MEMBER INSPECTION RIGHTS — CORPORATE AND LLC RECORDS INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Innovations, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — INSPECTION RIGHTS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet relates to Acme Innovations, Inc., a California corporation organized under the laws of California, and to Jordan Lee's status as a shareholder or member of Acme Innovations, Inc. It describes the statutory rights a California corporation's shareholder or a California LLC's member has to inspect and copy the entity's books, records, and minutes, along with the written-demand process those statutes describe and the remedy available if a demand is refused. Stated purpose for a records request under this information sheet, if one is being made: To review financial records relevant to a potential breach of fiduciary duty by a director.

This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself constitute a written demand on Acme Innovations, Inc., does not determine whether Jordan Lee's stated purpose is one a court would find "reasonably related" to their interest as a shareholder or member within the meaning of the statutes described below, and does not determine whether any ownership threshold that applies to a particular right described below is met. This document is not this project's Corporate Bylaws or Multi-Member LLC Operating Agreement document, which govern Acme Innovations, Inc.'s internal affairs generally; this document instead focuses specifically on the inspection-and-copying statutes.

SHAREHOLDER'S RIGHT TO INSPECT ACCOUNTING BOOKS, RECORDS, AND MINUTES
A California corporation's accounting books, records, and minutes of proceedings of the shareholders, the board, and board committees must be open to inspection at the corporation's principal office in California (or, if it has none, at its registered agent's location), on the written demand of any shareholder or voting trust certificate holder, at any reasonable time during usual business hours, for a purpose reasonably related to that person's interest as a shareholder or voting trust certificate holder. This right carries no minimum-ownership threshold — it belongs to any shareholder, whether they hold one share or many. As an alternative to inspecting in person, the shareholder or certificate holder can instead ask the corporation to produce the books, records, and minutes by mail or electronically, if they pay the reasonable cost of copying or converting the documents. The right extends to the records of each of the corporation's subsidiaries, and it may be exercised in person or through an agent or attorney, including the right to copy and make extracts.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The accounting books, records, and minutes of proceedings of the shareholders and the board and committees of the board of any domestic corporation, and of any foreign corporation keeping any records in this state or having its principal office in California, or a true and accurate copy thereof if the original has been lost, destroyed, or is not normally physically located within this state shall be open to inspection at the corporation’s principal office in California, or if none, at the physical location for the corporation’s registered agent for service of process in this state, upon the written demand on the corporation of any shareholder or holder of a voting trust certificate at any reasonable time during usual business hours, for a purpose reasonably related to the holder’s interests as a shareholder or as the holder of a voting trust certificate."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1601(a) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, shareholder right to inspect books, records, and minutes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1601.)
  "The inspection by a shareholder or holder of a voting trust certificate may be made in person or by agent or attorney, and the right of inspection includes the right to copy and make extracts. The right of the shareholders to inspect the corporate records may not be limited by the articles or bylaws."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1601(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, method of inspection and non-waivability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1601.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, unconditional shareholder right — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Unlike the shareholder-list right described elsewhere in this document (Corp. Code § 1600(a)), this records-and-minutes right under § 1601 carries no ownership-percentage or dollar-value threshold at all; a single share is enough, as long as the shareholder's purpose is reasonably related to their interest as a shareholder. This document doesn't resolve what counts as a "purpose reasonably related" to that interest in any specific case — that determination is fact-specific and, if contested, is for a court. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1601) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

SHAREHOLDER'S RIGHT TO INSPECT AND COPY THE SHAREHOLDER LIST
California corporate law gives two distinct rights covering the list of a corporation's shareholders, and they are not the same right. First, a shareholder or shareholders holding at least 5% in the aggregate of the corporation's outstanding voting shares — or holding at least 1% of those voting shares and having filed a Schedule 14A with the SEC — has an absolute right to inspect and copy the shareholder record (names, addresses, and shareholdings) during business hours, on five business days' prior written demand, or to obtain a compiled list of voting shareholders from the corporation's transfer agent on written demand and payment of the agent's usual charges. Separately, and without any ownership threshold at all, the shareholder record is also open to inspection and copying by any shareholder or voting trust certificate holder, at any time during usual business hours, on written demand, for a purpose reasonably related to that person's interest as a shareholder or certificate holder.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A shareholder or shareholders holding at least 5 percent in the aggregate of the outstanding voting shares of a corporation or who hold at least 1 percent of those voting shares and have filed a Schedule 14A with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission shall have an absolute right to do either or both of the following: (1) inspect and copy the record of shareholders’ names and addresses and shareholdings during usual business hours upon five business days’ prior written demand upon the corporation, or (2) obtain from the transfer agent for the corporation, upon written demand and upon the tender of its usual charges for such a list"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1600(a) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, ownership threshold for the streamlined shareholder-list right (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1600.)
  "The record of shareholders shall also be open to inspection and copying by any shareholder or holder of a voting trust certificate at any time during usual business hours upon written demand on the corporation, for a purpose reasonably related to such holder’s interests as a shareholder or holder of a voting trust certificate."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1600(c) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, general shareholder-list inspection right with no ownership threshold (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1600.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine ownership-linked right — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. It's worth stating precisely because it corrects a natural assumption: the 5%-or-1%-with-Schedule-14A threshold in subdivision (a) applies specifically to the streamlined, no-purpose-required procedure for getting a compiled shareholder list on five business days' notice (including from the transfer agent) — it is not the threshold for inspecting the shareholder record at all. Subdivision (c) gives every shareholder and voting trust certificate holder, regardless of how small their holding is, a separate right to inspect and copy that same shareholder record at any time during business hours, without the five-business-day mechanism, as long as their purpose is reasonably related to their interest as a shareholder. This document doesn't restate subdivision (b)'s separate remedy (a court order postponing a shareholders' meeting) for a corporation's delay in complying with a subdivision (a) demand. Citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1600) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

REMEDY FOR A CORPORATION'S REFUSAL TO PERMIT INSPECTION
If a corporation refuses a lawful demand for inspection, the superior court of the proper county may enforce the right of inspection on just and proper conditions, or, for good cause shown, appoint one or more competent inspectors or accountants to audit the corporation's books and records and investigate its property, funds, and affairs (including those of its subsidiaries), and report to the court. Officers and agents of the corporation must produce all books and documents in their custody to inspectors or accountants appointed this way, on penalty of contempt of court. The expenses of that investigation or audit are paid by the person who applied for it, unless the court orders the corporation to pay or share them.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Upon refusal of a lawful demand for inspection, the superior court of the proper county, may enforce the right of inspection with just and proper conditions or may, for good cause shown, appoint one or more competent inspectors or accountants to audit the books and records kept in this state and investigate the property, funds and affairs of any domestic corporation or any foreign corporation keeping records in this state and of any subsidiary corporation thereof, domestic or foreign, keeping records in this state and to report thereon in such manner as the court may direct."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1603(a) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, court enforcement of a refused inspection demand (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1603.)
  "All officers and agents of the corporation shall produce to the inspectors or accountants so appointed all books and documents in their custody or power, under penalty of punishment for contempt of court."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1603(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, duty to produce records to a court-appointed inspector (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1603.)
  "All expenses of the investigation or audit shall be defrayed by the applicant unless the court orders them to be paid or shared by the corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1603(c) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, who pays for the court-ordered audit (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1603.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual court remedy for a refused demand — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. It's worth stating precisely because it corrects a natural assumption: this statute does not create a fixed per-day or per-violation monetary penalty for refusing inspection (unlike some other California recordkeeping statutes, such as the wage-statement inspection right elsewhere in this project's corpus, which does carry a specific dollar penalty). The remedy here is a court order compelling inspection or an audit, with the cost of that audit defaulting to the person who sought it unless the court shifts it to the corporation — the statute does not by its own terms award the shareholder attorney's fees or other damages for the refusal itself. This document doesn't address whether a shareholder could pursue a different remedy (such as a general civil action) outside this specific statute. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1603) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

LLC MEMBER'S AND TRANSFEREE'S RIGHT TO INSPECT COMPANY RECORDS
Under the California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, each member, manager, and transferee of a California LLC has the right, on reasonable request and for purposes reasonably related to that person's interest as a member, manager, or transferee, to inspect and copy — during normal business hours — any of the records the LLC is statutorily required to maintain, and to obtain a written copy of the LLC's federal, state, and local income tax returns for each year, promptly after they become available. The records the LLC must maintain and make available for this purpose include a current alphabetical list of each member's and transferee's name, address, contribution, and share of profits and losses; the articles of organization and any amendments; the written operating agreement, if any, and its amendments; copies of the LLC's tax returns and financial statements for the six most recent fiscal years; and the LLC's internal-affairs books and records for at least the current and past four fiscal years.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Each member, manager, and transferee has the right, upon reasonable request, for purposes reasonably related to the interest of that person as a member, manager, or transferee, to each of the following: (1) To inspect and copy during normal business hours any of the records required to be maintained pursuant to Section 17701.13. (2) To obtain in writing from the limited liability company, promptly after becoming available, a copy of the limited liability company’s federal, state, and local income tax returns for each year."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.10(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, member and transferee inspection and tax-return rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.10.)
  "Each limited liability company shall maintain in writing or in any other form capable of being converted into clearly legible tangible form at the office referred to in subdivision (a) all of the following: (1) A current list of the full name and last known business or residence address of each member and of each transferee set forth in alphabetical order, together with the contribution and the share in profits and losses of each member and transferee."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.13(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the records an LLC must maintain and make available (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.13.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine default access right — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. This is the correct current citation for the LLC member/transferee inspection right itself (Corp. Code § 17704.10(b)); § 17701.13 is a distinct section that separately defines which records an LLC must maintain in the first place — § 17704.10(b) cross-references it rather than duplicating it, so both sections matter to understanding the full scope of what can be inspected. Like the corporate right described elsewhere in this document, this right is phrased around a "purpose reasonably related to the interest" of the person requesting it, and it belongs to a transferee (someone who has received an economic interest, such as an heir, without becoming a full member) as well as to members and managers — not only to those with voting or management rights. Unlike the corporate shareholder-list right described elsewhere in this document, this LLC right carries no minimum-ownership-percentage threshold. This document doesn't restate the additional annual and interim financial-reporting duties this same statute imposes once an LLC has more than 35 members. Citations below are from two separate statutory sections within the same LLC Act (§ 17704.10 and § 17701.13) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

THESE RIGHTS CAN'T BE LIMITED BY THE ENTITY'S OWN GOVERNING DOCUMENTS
Neither entity type lets its own governing documents cut back these inspection rights. For a California corporation, the statutes creating both the shareholder-list right and the books-records-and-minutes right each say directly that the right "may not be limited by the articles or bylaws." For a California LLC, the member/transferee inspection statute states even more broadly that "any waiver of the rights provided in this section shall be unenforceable" — not limited to a waiver in the articles of organization or operating agreement specifically. The LLC statute also gives a court a broader toolkit than the corporate remedy described elsewhere in this document: beyond enforcing the right itself, a court may award the person who brought the action their reasonable expenses, including attorney's fees, if it finds the LLC's noncompliance was without justification.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any inspection and copying under this section may be made in person or by agent or attorney. The rights provided in this section may not be limited by the articles or bylaws."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1600(d) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, shareholder-list right can't be limited by articles or bylaws (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1600.)
  "The inspection by a shareholder or holder of a voting trust certificate may be made in person or by agent or attorney, and the right of inspection includes the right to copy and make extracts. The right of the shareholders to inspect the corporate records may not be limited by the articles or bylaws."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1601(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, books-and-records right can't be limited by articles or bylaws (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1601.)
  "Any waiver of the rights provided in this section shall be unenforceable."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.10(h) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, waiver of the inspection right is unenforceable (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.10.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of a genuine non-waivability rule for both entity types — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation or LLC. The corporate non-waivability language (Corp. This document also doesn't address whether a corporation's shareholders agreement (a separate contract from the articles or bylaws) could have a different effect than the bylaws themselves on the corporate right, since the quoted statutes name only the articles and bylaws. The three citations below are drawn from two separate statutory sections of the corporate inspection chapter (§§ 1600, 1601) and one section of a separate LLC statute (§ 17704.10) — related but independently enacted provisions, not a single independently authored source, and not identical in scope to each other.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of a genuine non-waivability rule for both entity types — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation or LLC. The corporate non-waivability language (Corp. Code §§ 1600(d), 1601(b)) is textually narrower than the LLC's (§ 17704.10(h)): the corporate statutes bar limiting the right only through "the articles or bylaws," while the LLC statute bars "any waiver of the rights" without naming a specific document — this document doesn't resolve whether that difference in wording would actually produce a different outcome for, say, a side agreement that isn't part of the articles or bylaws. This document also doesn't address whether a corporation's shareholders agreement (a separate contract from the articles or bylaws) could have a different effect than the bylaws themselves on the corporate right, since the quoted statutes name only the articles and bylaws. The three citations below are drawn from two separate statutory sections of the corporate inspection chapter (§§ 1600, 1601) and one section of a separate LLC statute (§ 17704.10) — related but independently enacted provisions, not a single independently authored source, and not identical in scope to each other.
